approach: The authors conducted a narrative literature review, focusing on recent evidence (especially from the last two years prior to publication). They systematically categorized identified prognostic factors into distinct biological and clinical domains. For each category, they summarized findings from multiple independent patient cohorts and experimental studies, discussing associations with response rates, survival outcomes, and resistance mechanisms. The review also evaluated the practicality and problems of using these factors as routine clinical biomarkers.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides a structured synthesis of diverse prognostic factors for CPI efficacy, integrating clinical, genomic, microenvironmental, and microbiome data up to 2018.
contribution_and_limits.limits: As a narrative review, it does not present new primary data or perform meta-analyses; many cited biomarkers lack standardized measurement protocols or validation in large, heterogeneous cohorts; contradictory findings (e.g., in gut microbiota) highlight the need for further research.

key_findings.conditions: Across various cancer types treated with CPIs
key_findings.finding: Large individual differences exist in efficacy and adverse reactions; only a subset of patients respond objectively.

key_findings.conditions: Clinical factors: Age, Gender, Diet, Viral Infection
key_findings.finding: Elderly patients (≥75 years) may have reduced benefit and higher hyperprogression risk; males generally show greater benefit than females; obesity correlates with improved anti-PD therapy benefit in males; viral infections (MCV, EBV) are associated with better responses due to strong tumor-specific antigens.

key_findings.conditions: Tumor-autonomous: TMB, MSI, PD-L1, Gene Mutations
key_findings.finding: High TMB/MSI correlates with improved efficacy; PD-L1 expression is a widely used but imperfect biomarker (dynamic, threshold-dependent); specific mutations (e.g., EGFR, PTEN loss, JAK1/2, B2M) are linked to resistance or poor outcomes, while others (PBRM1, ARID2) may improve sensitivity.

High CD8+ TILs generally predict better response, though context matters (e.g., gastric cancer paradox); Tregs and MDSCs impair efficacy; IDO inhibition showed synergy in early trials but failed in Phase III; IFNγ signaling defects lead to resistance.

key_findings.conditions: Host Factors: Blood Markers, MHC, TCR
key_findings.finding: Low NLR, high eosinophils/lymphocytes, low LDH predict better survival; impaired MHC class I (e.g., B2M mutations) causes resistance; less diverse TCR repertoire is associated with response to anti-PD-1.

Specific bacteria (Bacteroides spp. for CTLA-4; Bifidobacterium, Akkermansia muciniphila, Ruminococcaceae for anti-PD-1) are associated with better responses; antibiotic use or dysbiosis leads to primary resistance; fecal microbiota transplantation can restore responsiveness in models.

problem_or_question: To identify and evaluate candidate prognostic factors that can serve as biomarkers for predicting the efficacy and adverse drug reactions of CPI-based immunotherapies, addressing the large individual differences in treatment outcomes observed in clinical practice.
research_scope: The review covers prognostic factors influencing the efficacy and adverse reactions of checkpoint inhibitor (CPI) based immunotherapy (anti-CTLA-4, anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1) across various advanced solid tumors. It synthesizes evidence from clinical trials and experimental investigations reported primarily within the two years preceding 2018.
work_summary: This paper provides a comprehensive update on the biomarkers and mechanisms associated with response to CPI-based immunotherapy. It categorizes prognostic factors into clinically relevant factors (age, gender, diet, viral infection), tumor-autonomous mechanisms (TMB, MSI, PD-L1 expression, gene mutations), tumor microenvironment components (immune cells, immunoregulatory pathways), host-related factors (peripheral blood markers, MHC class I, TCR repertoire, genetic signatures), and gut microbiota. The authors discuss the potential of these factors as biomarkers for precision medicine, highlighting both their predictive value and current limitations in clinical application.
